summary: Describes ICAP, the Internet Content Adaptation Protocol, a lightweight way to pass HTTP messages to servers that transform them, such as for virus scanning or content filtering. In essence it is remote procedure calls on HTTP messages. It is informational.

eli5.summary: A web proxy can hand a page to a helper that cleans or changes it, such as removing viruses, and then get it back. ICAP is how they talk.

questions: how does icap work with proxies
subtitle: Pass HTTP messages to external servers for transformation and adaptation.

tldr.problem: Web proxies and caches need to transform messages—scanning for viruses, filtering content, or adapting them for different devices—but cannot do all transformations internally.
tldr.mechanism: ICAP (Internet Content Adaptation Protocol) lets proxies send HTTP requests or responses to external ICAP servers over TCP, which process them and return adapted versions.
tldr.outcome: ICAP enables edge servers to perform heavy transformations on cached content without reloading from the origin, or to offload work like virus scanning to specialized servers. It saw real-world deployment despite being informational rather than standards-track.

today: RFC 3507 is an Informational specification, not a standards-track protocol. However, ICAP is widely deployed in commercial content filtering and optimization appliances. The RFC notes that the Open Pluggable Services (OPES) working group was chartered to produce a standards-track protocol for similar functions, but ICAP remained the existing, deployed solution. The document itself does not address architectural and policy issues described in later RFCs.

sections.title: Introduction and Use Cases
sections.content:
ICAP (Internet Content Adaptation Protocol) is a lightweight protocol that lets HTTP intermediaries like proxies and caches send messages to external servers for processing. It enables content transformation, filtering, and security checking without requiring all the logic to be built into the proxy itself.

The RFC identifies several key use cases. Content providers can use ICAP servers near the network edge to insert personalized advertisements into cached pages, avoiding the need to mark pages uncacheable and repeatedly fetch them from the origin. Surrogates can offload expensive operations like virus scanning to external servers, distributing the computational load. Firewalls and proxies can send requests to URI-checking services to enforce access policies, such as parental controls. Each scenario reduces load on origin servers or the network by enabling localized transformation.
sections.eli5: A proxy is like a gatekeeper between you and the internet. Sometimes it wants to change a web page before showing it to you, but it does not know how. ICAP lets it ask a helper server to do the work.

sections.title: Request and Response Modification
sections.content:
ICAP defines two main modes of operation. In request modification (REQMOD), the ICAP client (usually a proxy) sends an incoming HTTP request to an ICAP server, which can return a modified request, an HTTP error response, or a no-modification indication. The proxy then forwards the (possibly modified) request to the origin server. This is useful for filtering outgoing requests based on URI policies or modifying request headers.

In response modification (RESPMOD), the ICAP client sends an HTTP response from an origin server to an ICAP server, which processes it and returns an adapted version. The proxy then delivers the modified response to the downstream client. This mode supports virus scanning, content filtering, format conversion, and other post-processing on responses before they reach users.

The protocol allows ICAP servers to signal that no modification is needed with a 204 No Content response, which helps clients avoid buffering entire messages unnecessarily. Clients can also use message preview—sending just the headers and the first few kilobytes of a message—to let ICAP servers make a quick decision before committing to process the full content.
sections.eli5: There are two types of work. First, the proxy can ask the helper to check or change a request before it goes out—like checking what websites you are asking for. Second, it can ask the helper to fix a page coming back from the internet—like checking it for viruses.

sections.title: Protocol Structure and Messages
sections.content:
ICAP is a separate protocol from HTTP, not an application running over HTTP. It uses TCP/IP with a default port of 1344. ICAP messages follow the same structure as HTTP/1.1: a request or status line, headers, a blank line, and an optional body. The current version is ICAP/1.0.

A key feature is the Encapsulated header, which identifies what parts of the ICAP message body are encapsulated HTTP message sections. For example, Encapsulated: req-hdr=0, req-body=512 means the request headers start at byte 0 and the request body starts at byte 512. This allows ICAP servers to parse which parts are the HTTP request or response being processed. Encapsulated bodies use chunked transfer encoding, while encapsulated headers do not.

ICAP defines three methods: REQMOD (request modification), RESPMOD (response modification), and OPTIONS (configuration). All ICAP servers must support OPTIONS, which lets clients query the server for supported methods, preview size, and other capabilities. The OPTIONS response includes an ISTag (ICAP Service Tag)—a version identifier that clients can cache alongside previous ICAP responses to validate that cached results are still fresh.
sections.eli5: ICAP messages look like email: a header section with information, then a blank line, then the content. The header labels where the important parts are, like a table of contents. This helps both sides understand what they are looking at.

sections.title: Headers, URIs, and Service Configuration
sections.content:
ICAP requests are addressed using absolute URIs with the icap: scheme, for example icap://icap.example.net:2000/services/service-1. If no port is specified, port 1344 is assumed. ICAP URIs can include query parameters to pass service-specific arguments, like icap://icap.net/translate?lang=french.

ICAP supports standard HTTP headers like Cache-Control, Date, and Expires with the same semantics. Several headers are specific to ICAP. The Preview header in requests tells the server how many bytes of the encapsulated body will be sent before waiting for a response. The Allow: 204 header indicates the client can accept a 204 No Content response. Response headers include ISTag (a version tag for the service state) and standard HTTP status codes adapted for ICAP (for example, 404 means ICAP Service not found; 503 means Service overloaded).

Clients can use the OPTIONS method to discover what each ICAP service supports and how to use it. OPTIONS responses include the Methods header (which mode the service supports), Preview size recommendations, and Max-Connections limits. Options can include hints about which file types should be previewed (Transfer-Preview) or skipped entirely (Transfer-Ignore), allowing clients to optimize what they send.
sections.eli5: ICAP services have addresses on the internet, and clients ask them questions to learn what they can do. The answers tell the client how to talk to the service and what to expect.

sections.title: Security and Deployment Notes
sections.content:
The RFC emphasizes that transformations should generally only be performed with the explicit consent of either the content provider or the user. Without a policy framework, widespread deployment of unconsented transformations could yield unpredictable results. Authentication between ICAP client and server can use standard HTTP mechanisms. Encryption can be negotiated using the Upgrade header to enable Transport Layer Security on an ICAP connection.

ICAP clients should use the OPTIONS method before attempting unknown methods, as servers may return 501 Method Not Implemented for unsupported operations. The protocol also defines error-handling guidance: when an ICAP server returns an error, the client may return the error to the user, execute the unadapted request anyway, or retry the adaptation. For response modification errors specifically, the client should not pass ICAP errors directly downstream to users, since those errors only make sense in the ICAP transaction layer.

A critical implementation note is that ICAP uses chunked transfer encoding for encapsulated bodies (not for encapsulated headers). This is a deliberate choice documented in the RFC to allow clients to stream large bodies without knowing their total length in advance—important for proxies that receive responses from servers that do not send Content-Length.
sections.eli5: Using ICAP to change what people see on the internet can be risky if they do not know it is happening. The protocol lets both sides prove who they are and talk secretly, and defines rules for what should happen if something goes wrong.
